Furthermore, the latest Trustees Report estimates the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund (OASI) will exhaust its asset reserves -- the excess income collected since inception that's invested in special-issue, interest-bearing government bonds, as required by law -- by the fourth quarter of 2032. Although Social Security isn't going bankrupt, the existing payout schedule, including annual cost-of-living adjustments , appears unsustainable and may require sweeping benefit cuts in six years.
Image source: Official White House Photo.
Despite these challenges, President Donald Trump campaigned (for his second nonconsecutive term) on ending the taxation of Social Security benefits. Halting this highly unpopular tax would enable retirees to retain more of their monthly payout.
While the president's promise sounded great on paper, he ultimately failed to keep his pledge . Worse yet, his flagship tax and spending law, the "Big, Beautiful Bill," appears to have accelerated the OASI's path to insolvency.
In late July 2024, mere months before the election, then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump wrote in all caps on Truth Social, "Seniors should not pay tax on Social Security."
Though this wasn't an official policy proposal from candidate Trump, it set an expectation that, if elected, he would end the taxation of benefits.
Back in 1983, Social Security's trust funds (the OASI and the Disability Insurance trust fund) were running on fumes. Without reforms, the program's asset reserves would have been exhausted in less than a year. This led to the passage of the Social Security Amendments of 1983, which, among other things, introduced the taxation of benefits.
Beginning in 1984, up to 50% of an individual's benefits could be exposed to the federal income tax rate if their provisional income -- adjusted gross income + tax-free interest + one-half of benefits -- exceeded $25,000 (or $32,000 for a couple filing jointly). A second tax tier was added in 1993, exposing up to 85% of benefits to federal taxation when provisional income topped $34,000 for single filers or $44,000 for couples filing jointly.
When introduced, the tax on benefits affected about one in 10 senior households. But since these provisional income thresholds have never been adjusted for inflation, around 50% of all senior households now pay federal tax on some portion of their Social Security income.
President Trump claimed that his flagship tax and spending law, the Big, Beautiful Bill (signed July 4, 2025), ends the tax on Social Security income -- but this isn't the case.
The president's tax and spending law temporarily increases the annual standard deduction for eligible seniors aged 65 and over by $6,000 (or $12,000 if filing jointly) from calendar years 2025 through 2028. While this has reduced the federal income tax liability for some retirees, it's not an end to the taxation of benefits.
Even if President Trump wanted to end the taxation of benefits, it would have proved virtually impossible. It would take 60 of 100 votes in the Senate to amend the Social Security Act, and neither party has had a supermajority in the upper house of Congress since the late 1970s. Ending the taxation of benefits isn't an issue that would garner bipartisan support.
Long story short, President Trump failed to uphold his pledge to end Social Security taxation.
Image source: Getty Images.
On top of not sticking to his campaign promise of ending the tax on benefits, the president's Big, Beautiful Bill looks to have dug an even deeper hole for America's top retirement program.
There's no question that select groups of taxpayers are benefiting from the Big, Beautiful Bill. It made the personal income tax bracket reduction from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent and introduced several temporary tax credits and deductions from 2025 through 2028. In addition to the aforementioned senior deduction, which can provide a beefed-up annual deduction, Trump's tax law introduced the "no tax on tips" and "no tax on overtime" provisions for eligible workers.
But as the Big, Beautiful Bill giveth to taxpayers, it taketh away from Social Security.
Between 2025 and 2028, the temporary deductions associated with this law are reducing the pool of earned income (wages and salaries, but not investment income) subject to the 12.4% payroll tax. Last year, this payroll tax brought in more than 91% of Social Security's income.
Shortly after President Trump signed the Big, Beautiful Bill into law, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) requested that the Social Security Administration (SSA) provide a 10-year projection of how it would affect the program. In early August 2025, the SSA's Office of the Actuary (OACT) published its findings.
The OACT estimates that Trump's tax and spending law will add $168.6 billion in costs to Social Security from 2025 through 2034. Additionally, the OACT predicted that the OASI's asset reserve insolvency would shift forward by three months, from the first quarter of 2033 to the fourth quarter of 2032. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the OASI's asset reserve insolvency timeline moved from the first quarter of 2033 to the fourth quarter of 2032 in the 2026 Social Security Board of Trustees Report.
The law that President Trump claimed ended the taxation of benefits (but didn't) is accelerating the timeline for sweeping benefit cuts for retired workers and survivors of deceased workers.
If you're like most Americans, you're a few years (or more) behind on your retirement savings. But a handful of little-known "Social Security secrets" could help ensure a boost in your retirement income. For example: one easy trick could pay you as much as $23,760 more ... each year! Once you learn how to maximize your Social Security benefits, we think you could retire confidently with the peace of mind we're all after.

Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has wrapped up a brief visit to the Philippines and is heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.
On his one-night visit to Manila, Carney attended a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, announced the conclusion of free-trade negotiations with the Philippines and unveiled funding for protecting tropical rainforests.
“What Canada presents is certainty to the world,” Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.
Carney was among foreign leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump who were invited to the summit by the Philippine chair, who is holding the rotating presidency of ASEAN, a bloc of 11 countries.
Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with ASEAN, which Sidhu said would give Canada access to smaller countries, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.
“You can get more into the weeds. You can upgrade later on, when you’re dealing with (one deal that is) bilateral, as opposed to an agreement with 11 partners,” he said in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.
“It’s the fastest growing region in the world, 700 million consumers, an economy valued at $6 trillion.”
Sidhu also expressed confidence for Canadian pork producers, as the Philippines moves toward restricting pork imports from a wide array of countries, including Canada.
“They’ve got a global safeguards investigation … for 60 days. Canada is not the culprit, and you’ll find out once the investigation is done,” he said.
Carney also met meet with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on the sidelines of the summit, where he announced $540 million for an initiative to protect rainforests, as part of a project co-led by Brazil and Norway.
The money is part of a $6 billion fund promised by Ottawa this spring in support for international climate finance. It is meant to attract public and private investment for preserving biodiversity and supporting communities that rely on these ecosystems.
Through an interpreter, Lula described the money as investments that will yield a profit and not “donations, money for free.”
Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.
“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.
Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.
While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.
“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.
Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.
Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.
He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.
“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.
“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”
The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.
“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, on pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.
Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

Ukrainian investigator Solomiya Khoma tells Fox News Digital how alleged recruiters and Russian cultural groups draw young African women into Russia’s military-industrial workforce as new agreements with African governments raise concerns.
Two African governments have signed new agreements with a Russian industrial complex linked to the production of attack drones used against Ukraine, even as a Ukrainian investigation alleges Moscow is expanding a recruitment network that draws young African women into its military-industrial workforce.
The agreements, signed in late October by Ghana and the Democratic Republic of the Congo with Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, come months after Britain sanctioned individuals and entities associated with the Alabuga Start program over deceptive recruitment practices. The new partnerships raise questions about whether Russia's efforts to attract foreign workers could help sustain drone production as its war against Ukraine continues.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre says it has obtained internal documents identifying approximately 50 African women employed at Alabuga, alongside 10 Russian recruiters and two African intermediaries allegedly involved in attracting foreign workers.
OUR ADVERSARIES ARE EVEN USING THE US BANKING SYSTEM. HERE’S HOW THEY GET AWAY WITH IT
The remains of a Russian-made, Iran-designed Shahed-136 drone, known in Russia as a Geran-2, are displayed with other recovered drones, glide bombs, missiles and rockets in Kharkiv on July 30, 2025. (Scott Peterson/Getty Images)
"What we were able to do is basically to obtain internal documentation," Solomiya Khoma, the organization's head of international cooperation, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
Khoma said the investigation went beyond previous reporting by attempting to establish how recruitment operates across borders, connecting Russian cultural organizations, local intermediaries and Alabuga's human resources department. "Our case is specifically related to African countries," she said.
According to the report, the alleged network operates on three levels: Russian cultural and educational organizations cultivating relationships with young people in Africa, local recruiters promoting opportunities abroad, and Alabuga personnel arranging employment and logistics.
A satellite image shows possible planned location of UAV manufacturing plant in Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, as evidence of new Russian-Iran cooperation, in this handout acquired June 9, 2023. (White House/Handout via Reuters)
The investigation identifies two women from Tunisia and Uganda as alleged recruitment coordinators and describes connections with Russian HR personnel and foreign employees. Their specific recruitment activities have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.
Khoma said the findings relied partly on a confidential source who remains employed within the Alabuga industrial complex.
"This person is still continuing to work in the Alabuga economical zone and these factories," she said, explaining why the organization could not disclose the source's identity.
She said investigators obtained information about the workers and their identities, including internal employee passes.
The researchers also examined the involvement of Russian cultural organizations, including councils of Russian compatriots and the Russkiy Mir Foundation, in promoting educational and employment opportunities in African countries.
The report points to a September 2024 cooperation memorandum between the Russian compatriots' council in Tunisia and Alabuga, alongside Russian cultural activities in Uganda. However, the investigation does not establish that Russian diplomats or cultural organizations knowingly directed recruits into military drone production.
The findings build on an Associated Press investigation published in October 2024 , which documented how African women recruited with promises of education and civilian employment were assigned to manufacture Iranian-designed attack drones . Some described long hours, lower-than-promised wages, surveillance and exposure to hazardous chemicals.
Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the Democratic Republic of the Congo's President Felix Tshisekedi arrive for their meeting on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia, October 30, 2026. (Pavel Bednyakov/Pool via Reuters)
Khoma described a recruitment process in which women arrive in Russia expecting to combine education with paid employment, only to fail entrance examinations or Russian-language requirements.
"These people are promised a dual education opportunity," she said.
After failing examinations, she alleged, workers may find themselves with limited options and unable to afford transportation home, leaving them performing factory work instead of pursuing their expected studies.
The recruitment program has also attracted international scrutiny. On May 5, 2026, the British government sanctioned seven individuals and entities associated with Alabuga Start recruitment, accusing the operation of using deceptive practices to obtain foreign labor for facilities producing military drones.
Yet cooperation with African governments appears to be continuing.

Ghanaian broadcaster Citi News reported October 29 that Labor Minister Emmanuel Agyekum signed an agreement with Alabuga to facilitate industrial employment opportunities for Ghanaian citizens. The ministry said it would coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation.
Meanwhile, CongoRassure reported October 30 that the Democratic Republic of the Congo signed a five-year memorandum focused on vocational training and strengthening employment institutions.
Russia's President Vladimir Putin and Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama enter a hall before the beginning of their talks on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Russia, October 30, 2026. (Anastasia Barashkova/Pool/Reuters)
Neither agreement, as publicly described, establishes that either government intended to supply workers for military production.
Khoma called for sanctions targeting the recruitment networks themselves, including intermediaries, financial channels and organizations facilitating foreign labor recruitment.
She argued that Russia's efforts to attract workers from abroad reflect growing labor shortages across its wartime economy and represent another potential point of international pressure.

articles.title_orig: 5 Tips And Tricks Every PS5 Owner Should Know
articles.title_zh: 5 Tips And Tricks Every PS5 Owner Should Know
articles.content_orig:
The PS5 has several quality-of-life features that save time and reduce annoyances.
When you fire up your PlayStation 5, you presumably want to get into a game instead of messing around in menus. Unless you're waiting for an update to install, you probably aren't eager to see what's buried within the Settings tab. But if you're a new PlayStation 5 owner or it's been a while since you tweaked your settings, you may have overlooked important options that make every play session better.
The PS5 has several quality-of-life features that are buried deep but have been expanded over the years. While the default options of the console aren't inherently bad, they can waste your console space, send unnecessary alerts and prevent the console's standout features from working at their best.
These options save time, reduce annoyances and make sure you're getting the most out of your console, so try them out for a superior experience.
By default, your PS5 captures a screenshot and video every time you earn a trophy. While it's cool to save a record of major achievements, not all trophy rarities deserve a video clip. These can quickly eat up a lot of storage space, especially if you play many different games and go for trophies.
To change this, go to Settings > Captures and Broadcasts > Captures > Trophies . I recommend setting Save Trophy Videos to Platinum, Gold so you save big moments without flooding your system with videos for random bronze trophies. Set the Trophy Video Duration to 15 seconds to save space unless you want the longer 30 seconds for full context.
While screenshots don't take up as much space as videos, adjusting the Save Trophy Screenshots option is also worthwhile if you don't care about those.
Two of the DualSense controller's standout features are its improved rumble and adaptive triggers. While many games let you turn these off entirely, if you find them overwhelming, try adjusting their intensity instead of outright shutting them off. Head to Settings > Accessories > Controller , where you're able to change Vibration Intensity and Trigger Effect Intensity .
Also in this menu, adjust Brightness of Controller Indicators if you find the colored light bar on the controller too dim or bright. Not every game uses this, but it can be distracting to see a constant red light while you're at low health, for example.
The PS5 controller has a mic built-in , which can work as a backup if your headset is dead. But when this mic is active, your system reduces the vibration and adaptive trigger intensity to minimize the amount of noise it picks up. To avoid this, go to Settings > Sound > Microphone and change Set Microphone Status When Logged In to Mute . This also prevents you from accidentally sharing audio in an online game. And if you ever need to mute all sound coming from your PS5, press and hold the Mute button for a moment.
By default, the Create button's behavior is awkward; you have to hold it for a second to take a screenshot, so it's easy to miss the moment you meant to capture. To make it more natural, visit Settings > Captures and Broadcasts > Shortcuts for Create button and choose Easy Screenshots . With this, pressing the button once takes a screenshot, while holding the button brings up the Create menu for full options.
Your PS5 sends various notifications that can be annoying when they come at the wrong times. It's nice to know a close friend just came online so you can invite them to a party, but you don't need a sale alert distracting you from an emotional cutscene. To control what notifications you get and when, go to Settings > Notifications . The top options control whether alerts appear at all, as well as whether they include a preview of their information and how long they stick on the screen.
Once you've set those, go through the list and choose to hide them when you're playing a game, watching media or live streaming. For example, you can hide game invites while watching Netflix so you don't get spammed by your friends and turn off useless ones like Feedback . Don't miss the When Friends Go Online option so you know when a multiplayer buddy is ready.
If you miss a notification, hit the PS Button on your controller to open the control center, then choose the Bell icon to view your alert history. You can also activate Do Not Disturb here to pause all notifications until you restart or turn this off.
When it comes to the control center, you aren't stuck with its default layout. After opening it with the PS button , press the Options button to show its customization panel. Select an item to move it to another position, or drop it down to Hidden Controls if you don't need it (though not all items can be hidden). There are also a few extra items not shown by default, like accessibility and network options. Adjust the utility to show what you use most so you spend less time fumbling around.
Over the years, the PS5 has added more home screen personalization as well. It's nothing like the custom themes of the PS3 and PS4, but can at least make your console feel more inviting. To start, select the Welcome Hub icon, represented by the four PlayStation symbols on the home screen.
At the top-right, you'll see four icons that let you select and move widgets, pick a preset arrangement, choose a wallpaper and adjust options. The widgets include quick views of your console's free space, online friends, controller battery level, recent screenshots and more — great for keeping relevant info all in one place so you don't have to dig into menus as often. For a bit of nostalgia, you can also change the PS5's interface and sound effects to use one of the four prior console generations . Head to Settings > System > Appearance > Appearance and Sound to take a look.
Finally, if you play a lot of different games, you should pin your favorites on the home screen so you don't have to dig them out of your library. Highlight a title, then hit the Options button on your controller. Choose Keep in Home from the resulting menu, and the game will stay as one of the icons on your home screen. You can't pin more than five items at a time.
If you're not a fan of the PS5's startup beep alerting others of your late-night gaming sessions, you can quiet or silence it at Settings > System > Beep and Light . The default Volume is High , but you can choose Low or enable the Mute Beep Sound toggle. In the same menu, select Brightness to customize how bright the PS5 console's lights are. Maybe you want the orange rest mode light bright for a makeshift nightlight or to dim the light to avoid distractions while playing.
You can set your preferred settings at the system level and supported games will use these without you having to configure them every time. This is under Settings > Saved Data and Game/App Settings > Game Presets . Available tweaks include difficulty, performance/resolution modes, camera inversion and subtitles. It saves time not having to configure these common options every time you start a new game.
Finally, if you use headphones, it's worth setting up 3D Audio for a more immersive experience. Go to Settings > Sound > 3D Audio (Headphones) > Create Personalized 3D Audio Profile to walk through a process to dial this in for your ears. It depends on your specific hearing, so test it out and see if you can hear in-game goings-on better than with stereo.

articles.title_orig: Three commercial vessels struck by drones near Romania's black sea, PM says
articles.title_zh: Three commercial vessels struck by drones near Romania's black sea, PM says
articles.content_orig:
BUCHAREST — Drones have ​struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal, Prime ‌Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice.
Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships’ crews had managed to control the fires ​on board after the strikes late on Saturday.
A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ​ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war ⁠between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance ​in the Black Sea.
The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane that links ​the Danube River to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports.
Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“These ​incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. “They reflect the ​deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.”
Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbours with drones.
Oprea ‌said ⁠the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis.
Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the ​Sulina canal, the defence ​ministry said, inside Romanian ⁠territorial waters.
Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television ​station Digi24 said the vessel was the Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa ​1.
“On Tuesday ⁠and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers,” Oprea said.
“We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through ⁠equipment for ​counter-drone warfare.”
France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols ​aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement.
Many of the ships hit in October and November were anchored near ​or sailing to or from the Sulina canal.

articles.title_orig: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.title_zh: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.content_orig:
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube channel of his lawyer
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?
A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government force retreats from strait in major setback in war against Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government force retreats from strait in major setback in war against Houthis
articles.content_orig:
Forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they are withdrawing from territory near the Bab al-Mandeb strait to focus on defending the interim capital, Aden, from the Houthi armed group.
A spokesman for the Southern Armed Forces, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, said on Sunday that it was redeploying from Dhubab airport and areas around Bab al-Mandeb in southwestern Yemen.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the spokesman said.
The announcement raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast, the base of the internationally recognised government since the Houthis drove leaders from the capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
Reinforcements would also be sent to try to end the Houthis’ siege of Taiz, where fighting has been raging to the west of the city, the announcement added.
Humanitarian conditions are worsening in Yemen’s third-largest city, with aid supplies blocked from entering and civilians unable to leave.
The city hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen since the 2022 ceasefire collapsed this summer and fighting surged. The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized large areas of territory along Yemen’s western coast in September.
Sunday’s announcement could signal a setback for the Yemeni government forces’ counteroffensive launched in September to reclaim areas seized by Houthi fighters.
The counteroffensive quickly recaptured key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to push the Houthis out of the key city of Mocha and other areas near the coast.
The Houthis responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights and targeting energy facilities.
Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, the Saudi capital. Later, coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said two drones launched over the Mecca region and another over the Medina region. The Houthis denied the allegations they attacked Mecca as “a blatant lie”.
Houthi forces also captured highland areas north of Aden, where the government has been operating since 2015, and say they are preparing to advance on the city itself.
A spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majid Al-Nazili, called on the international community to help return Bab al-Mandeb and Yemen’s west coast to government control, stressing that the strait was of vital importance for freedom of maritime navigation and international trade.
Separately, Yemen’s armed forces said that they had launched 906 strikes against Houthi positions, including 41 air strikes, on Marib, al-Jawf and Taiz.
Also on Sunday, the International Committee of the Red Cross announced that the Houthis, with its support, unilaterally released 600 prisoners “in connection with the armed conflict”.

articles.title_orig: Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships
articles.title_zh: Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships
articles.content_orig:
Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu on Sunday condemned drone strikes on three commercial ships near his country's Black Sea coast, promising to work with NATO allies to strengthen security in the region following the latest attacks.
“These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said in a post on X. He added that Russia's war against Ukraine was causing the security situation in the Black Sea to deteriorate.
The ships were hit Saturday evening and overnight near Sulina, a Romanian port where the Danube River meets the Black Sea.
The Greek-flagged oil tanker Evia Petrol V was struck just after 9 p.m., followed 35 minutes later by a strike on another ship, the Marsol, according to a statement from Romania's defense ministry published on its Facebook page.
“In both cases, the fires were extinguished by the ships' crews. No casualties were reported,” the ministry said.
A third vessel, the Ali Najafov, also reported being struck overnight. It remains unclear who launched the drones.
Romania's military detected aerial targets on radar and sent F-16 fighter jets into the air. Authorities also issued warnings to residents near the coast about possible drone threats.
The attacks came after another commercial ship, the Larissa 1, was reportedly hit by a drone near Romania's coast on Friday.
Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea said Sunday he would raise the incidents with allied counterparts in Brussels. “We need the solidarity of our allies,” he said, calling for more surveillance aircraft and equipment to defend against drones.
Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs following recent attacks on commercial shipping.
In October, at least seven commercial vessels were struck by drones in the Black Sea close to NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria, leaving more than 20 sailors dead and dozens missing.

articles.title_zh: US, China, Russia plan unprecedented meeting at APEC
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.title_zh: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.content_orig:
A Turkish man sentenced to life in prison for pushing his pregnant wife to her death off a famed 1,000-foot cliff for a life insurance policy payout was set free after only six years, sparking intense backlash.
Hakan Aysal was freed from a high-security prison as Turkey’s Supreme Court’s Criminal General Assembly reviews an appeal on the convicted killer’s lifetime sentence for the 2018 death of his wife, Semra Aysal, Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet reported Friday.
“My client’s six years of unjust imprisonment, approximately four of which he spent in solitary confinement, has come to an end,” Aysal’s lawyer said, according to the outlet.
Aysal, 45, was serving an aggravated life imprisonment sentence for the premeditated killing of his 32-year-old wife, whom he shoved off the scenic Butterfly Valley cliff after taking selfies together.
Aysal was convicted in October 2022.
Aysal’s lawyers and Supreme Court Chief Prosecutor Ömer Taş claimed there was a lack of sufficient, convincing evidence to convict the killer husband.
Turkish prosecutors had argued that Aysal shoved his wife, who was seven months pregnant with the couple’s child, while they were at the popular destination near the city of Muğla in southwestern Turkey.
Prosecutors told the court that Aysal had taken out a $25,000 accident insurance policy in his wife’s name, making himself the sole beneficiary and collecting the funds immediately after her death.
Aysal – who once attempted to enter a plea of insanity – has maintained his innocence, claiming he never pushed his wife and instead she had disappeared after he turned his back on her for a second.
A witness, who had recorded a video capturing the final moments of Semra Aysal on the cliff, said the husband had appeared “unusually calm” after the incident.
“We even joked, ‘Either this man will throw the woman off or the woman will throw the man.’ There was no interaction between them,'” witness Recep Sahin told police after he shared the footage with them.
Pro-women rights groups were outraged following the court’s decision to release Aysal as they review his appeal.
“The decision is extremely worrying, not only for this case but also in terms of the evaluation of evidence in femicide cases and the debates surrounding impunity,” lawyer Hediye Gökçe Baykal told Cumhuriyet.
The women’s wing of the New Party, Turkey’s social democratic political faction, called for justice for both Semra Aysal and her unborn child.
“A woman and her seven-month-old unborn baby lost their lives. The defendant, who received an aggravated life sentence, is now free,” the party wrote, according to the outlet.
“The Supreme Court has issued a release order for Hakan Aysal, who was sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for being responsible for the death of his wife, Semra Aysal, in Muğla. We ask: How will accountability be provided for the deaths of Semra and her unborn baby?” the group questioned.

articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

articles.title_orig: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.title_zh: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.content_orig:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

articles.title_orig: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters on Saturday that “both sides” – Kyiv and Moscow – know that compromises will be necessary to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on the next steps.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

articles.title_orig: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.title_zh: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.content_orig:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat, during a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese.
About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, located in a remote part of the Andes mountains of northern Peru, but the Pope's visit still drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.
At an outdoor Mass, the Pope spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages" and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.
More than 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.
In his sermon, the Pope thanked those who had made the journey to see him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.
The pontiff's Latin America tour comes roughly a month after he underwent surgery to remove part of his right lung after a cancerous lump was found during routine checks.
At the start of his trip, he said the care he had received made him think of those who "lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment for health conditions.
Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where the Pope served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.
On Saturday, he returned by helicopter and was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, from which he waved to people who had travelled to see him.
Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the 71-year-old said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.
"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.
Rev Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.
He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert', as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.
The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.
The US-born Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco and then on to a Peruvian section of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point he will return to Rome.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The Kremlin also confirmed the meeting on Saturday.
Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks and is also set to bring up the war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine , officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Mr. Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Mr. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which then-U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.
"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Howard Lutnick in the hot seat as lawmakers demand answers on Nvidia sales to China
articles.title_zh: Howard Lutnick in the hot seat as lawmakers demand answers on Nvidia sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times
By Ana Swanson Tripp Mickle Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company , sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.
