articles.title_orig: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.title_zh: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.content_orig:
Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they recovered from Friday's nationwide ground stop, but the FAA said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
More than 5,000 U.S. flights had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , already past the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted. Flight-tracking app Flighty said the outage has now caused more cancellations than the 2024 CrowdStrike software failure. "I do think the worst is behind us," Bedford said, and he apologized to travelers.
The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. About 12,000 flights couldn't be completed, Bedford said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began while L3Harris Technologies, which runs the network, was doing routine work to switch lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. A router involved in the work flooded the rest of the system, disrupting communications with airplanes and radar. Duffy said officials are working to determine "whether we had incompetence" by the contractor or a faulty router. "Until I can build" a new network, he said, "I'm stuck with L3Harris." Bedford said the review will determine whether the router was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective.
In a statement to Yahoo News, L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation" and "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." The company did not address Duffy's criticism or say what went wrong.
Asked why the work was done on a Friday afternoon, Duffy said work at small, remote sites is done during the day because it isn't expected to affect the wider system. "There'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work," he said. Bedford said maintenance on the network is logged on paper, so officials had to search through paper records to figure out who was working where.
Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told Yahoo News that communications with some planes were disrupted during the outage and that controllers moved flights to working frequencies. Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, he said, "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky."
The network's problems aren't new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris' predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review .
Duffy is pressing Congress for more money to replace the system. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy has said he wants $50 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. Bedford said the router swap was routine maintenance, not part of that modernization effort.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation .
Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and most major airlines are offering travel waivers. Airlines' promises of hotels and meals generally cover only disruptions within their control, which doesn't include an FAA ground stop.
National Air Traffic Controllers Association President Nick Daniels speaks during a news conference at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on September 28, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The head of the air traffic controllers' union told Yahoo News in a phone interview Saturday that communications with some planes were disrupted during Friday's outage. Controllers across the country had to scramble to keep flights moving safely, he said.
"We had controllers working with one another across the United States to see whose frequencies were working, whose radar was working," said Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association. Controllers checked whether they could hand off planes to one another if their own frequencies went down, he said.
Daniels said he hadn't reviewed the FAA's safety data. But asked what controllers had told him, he said, "We know we didn't have communications with airplanes, or that we were switching airplanes to different frequencies because their communications were being disrupted." Controllers "ensured the safety of every aircraft," he said.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a news conference earlier Saturday that "no facilities went dark," but acknowledged reports of "certain frequencies that were going in and out."
Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, Daniels said it depends on the risk. "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky," he said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that work at small, remote sites is routinely done during the day and that the practice will be reevaluated.
Daniels said such failures often happen when the FAA's required safety reviews before maintenance aren't followed. He said he didn't know whether that happened Friday.
Daniels wouldn't say whether Duffy was right to blame contractor L3Harris. "I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things," Daniels said. He said the union has warned for more than a decade that the system is failing, noting that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases to update computers.
Daniels said any new money for the air traffic control system should also go toward controllers' pay and working conditions. He said he hasn't spoken with Duffy since the outage, but that Duffy "already knows" the union's position. "We're going to continue working on that with this administration," he said.
More than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had predicted 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations for the day.
American has canceled the most flights, 892, followed by Delta (734), United (733) and Southwest (540). JetBlue has canceled 43% of its schedule.
The air traffic control system itself appears to be running near normal, and no airports had ground stops in effect Saturday afternoon. The problem now is getting planes and crews back where they're supposed to be.
Sunday looks better so far. About 130 U.S. flights scheduled for Sunday had been canceled as of Saturday afternoon.
L3Harris Technologies said Saturday it is supporting the FAA's investigation into Friday's outage. Earlier that day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly questioned whether the company's "incompetence" caused the outage.
"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," an L3Harris spokesperson said in a statement to Yahoo News. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
The company said that, "together with its telco partners and the FAA," it has completed more than 70% of the planned switch from copper wire to fiber optic lines. The statement doesn't say what caused the outage or respond to Duffy's suggestion of contractor error.
Asked whether L3Harris employees or a partner company did Friday's work, and whether the company disputes Duffy's suggestion of contractor error, a spokesperson said the company had nothing to offer beyond its statement.

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_zh: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.content_orig:
"The airlines are trying to get back to normal."
As air travel in the United States remains hectic due to the lingering effects from Friday's ground stop , a travel expert said preparation and patience are key for flyers who are trying to reach their destination.
Brett Snyder, the president of the travel planning service Cranky Concierge, said that flight schedules will likely not be back to normal until Monday at the earliest as airlines scramble to get their fleets and crews back to their planned destinations as orderly as possible.
A total of over 14,000 flights were canceled Friday and Saturday, according to FlightAware. Around 160 flights on Sunday have been canceled as of Saturday afternoon, FlightAware said.
The FAA said the ground stop was instituted due to a telecommunications issue in the air traffic control system.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the system is expected to be fully recovered by Sunday.
"The point of the cancellations and delays today is to right the ship as quick as possible and by Monday everything is as smooth as possible," Snyder told ABC News Saturday.
Snyder said that while there's not a lot passengers can do while the airlines and airports recover, there are key steps they can take to help ensure their flights go as smooth as possible.
The first thing that flyers should consider is if it's worth waiting for their flight if it has been delayed or if they should rebook, he said.
"If this was a trip that was going to be short and fun and not a big deal, I'd scrap it," Snyder said.
Snyder said that most airlines are offering refunds during this situation, even if their planned flight is delayed.
American Airlines announced Saturday it is adding fare caps across their domestic and short international flights as delays are expected to continue. American, Southwest, Delta and United are all offering travelers waivers.
Travelers are entitled to refunds for flights canceled by the airlines, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.
"The consumer is entitled to a refund if the airline cancelled a flight, regardless of the reason, and the consumer chooses not to travel or accept travel credits, vouchers, or other forms of compensation offered by the airline," DOT says on its website .
Additionally, travelers are entitled to a refund if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and they choose not to accept credits, vouchers or other compensation offered by the airline.
DOT defines a significantly delayed flight as three or more hours after the original scheduled arrival time for domestic flights.
For those who are still pushing ahead with their trip, Snyder said it's best to stay at the airport and remain on top of any updates. He recommended travelers download the airline's app and keeping an eye on all the alerts associated with their flight.
Snyder noted that flyers should pay close attention to any connecting flights and check if they are canceled. Airlines are typically good at rebooking customers during those situations, he added.
When in doubt, Snyder recommended that flyers call their airlines. If they are in the airport, talk to an agent, he said.
He stressed that ticket holders should remain courteous to the representatives.
"Remember the airline employees are going through this just as much you are as a traveler. Go easy on them, they're trying to help you," Snyder said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Saturday that the federal government is working around the clock to help the airlines and airports navigate through the issues and get service back to normal as fast as possible.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Duffy said in a post on X earlier Saturday.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said.

articles.title_orig: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.title_zh: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.content_orig:
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop just after 8 p.m. on Friday
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Thousands of travelers across the New York area are grappling with the effects of a nationwide ground stop, with nearly 2,000 flights canceled across the country on Saturday.
The disruptions are being felt across the region at Newark Liberty International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, and LaGuardia Airport, as passengers face delays, cancellations, and uncertain travel plans. Officials are hoping operations return to normal before the busy Thanksgiving travel period begins.
Port Authority released a statement Saturday saying,
"Travelers should anticipate continued delays and cancellations at the region's airports throughout the weekend as airlines recover from Friday night's nationwide FAA ground stop. By the end of Friday evening, JFK, LaGuardia, and New York Stewart airports had reported more than 800 cancellations and more than 600 delays.
Airlines are continuing to work through the logistical challenges created by Friday's disruption. Planes were left out of position across the country, and some flight attendants reached their allowable duty limits, requiring carriers to reassign crews and equipment before flights can return to normal schedules.
15% of flights were canceled out of Newark Saturday, 21% at LaGuardia, and 21% at JFK Airport. There were dozens of delays at all three airports.
On Friday evening at LaGuardia, one of the nation's busiest transportation hubs, only a handful of international flights were arriving after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to stop departing.
Video from the airport around 4:30 p.m. showed aircraft on the runway. About 30 minutes later, roughly a dozen planes were stopped in place as pilots received instructions to return to their gates.
"Nobody is allowed to leave the ground. If you are on the ground, please return to the gate immediately," pilots were told.
Even after flights resumed, some travelers remained stranded or scrambling to adjust their plans.
One passenger trying to reach Belize said the disruption left him frustrated after he missed his flight.
"Unfortunately, we did not make over our flight ... hopefully make it home," he said.
The FAA said it issued the nationwide ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday.
"We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was," Bedford said.
"When we have that root cause analysis complete, we'll share it with you," Bedford said.
He predicted the air travel schedule would fully recover by Sunday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does not believe the failure in communications that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday was the result of a cyber attack.
"In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber," Duffy said during a press conference Saturday.
Duffy said this transfer from copper to fiber has been happening in the U.S. for decades, saying virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital.
"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. So specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was gave us issues with our our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds," Duffy said.
When that happened the airspace was shut down for safety, Duffy said.
"Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online, so we don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet, didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul released a statement saying: "America's airspace ground to a halt yesterday, leaving thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded across the country. More than 3,500 planes were already in the air as radar and communications systems faltered. We're fortunate no lives were lost.
"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy's watch.
"Through it all, he's been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency.
"With millions of Americans preparing to travel for the holidays, families deserve answers and confidence in the safety of our skies. Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again.
"Sean Duffy must resign, or President Trump must remove him immediately."
Major airlines have issued travel waivers for affected passengers this weekend.
American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are waiving change fees through Saturday, with United also waiving fare differences. Southwest Airlines is allowing passengers to rebook at no additional cost through Monday.
Travelers are encouraged to check directly with their airline and review the status of their itinerary before heading to the airport as carriers continue working to minimize delays and cancellations.
The disruption marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last nationwide ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.content_orig:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.

She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.content_orig:
By OLIVIA CHRISTIE, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 10:06 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 12:49 EST, 14 November 2026
Andy Burnham claimed today that Britain has ‘lost more than we gained’ in the decade since the Brexit referendum – as he pressed ahead with his push for closer ties with Brussels.
Ahead of meeting European leaders at a UK-EU summit next week, the Prime Minister said a new deal he hopes to secure will ‘get food prices down’ and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.
Mr Burnham is expected to sign new agreements on food, emissions trading and youth mobility – arguing that he could strike a ‘win-win’ deal that could increase GDP by 0.4 per cent. He has said he will then ‘explore options’ for a different long-term relationship with the trading bloc.
But critics say the ‘reset’ could cost the UK £750million a week in membership fees and force us to adopt a new EU regulation every 12 hours.
Speaking at Welsh Labour conference today, the PM said: ‘We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.
‘It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU.
‘Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.
‘I want to remove some of the red tape that food exporters here face when they are seeking to send their product support abroad, but more than anything I’m trying to get prices down, food prices down, and if we get the right deal, that is what we will do, as well as reduce costs for businesses, and overall get more growth into the UK economy, up to 0.4 per cent on GDP.’
Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaking during the Welsh Labour conference today
He added: 'Why wouldn't I do that as Prime Minister? Why wouldn't I lead in that way? We've got the Conservatives who are standing out against it, saying no change. Well, I don't believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain.
'I think we've lost more than we've gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I'm going to lead as Prime Minister on this issue, and I'm going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.'
His comments come after a new campaign group claimed that the bill for Britain to re-join the EU would be a staggering £750million a week .
The group, Stay Out, blames Brussels' spiralling budget, a doubling of its borrowing costs and no chance of recovering the UK's special rebate negotiated by former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
The cost warning has echoes of Vote Leave's controversial campaign bus slogan, suggesting £350million per week could be clawed back from the EU and spent on the NHS. The Stay Out study reveals that the size of the EU’s annual budget has doubled since then and could land us with annual payments of £39.3billion a year.
Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart said Mr Burnham's focus on the future of the UK-EU relationship was a tactic to distract from rising welfare costs and questions about defence funding.
'Nearly a decade after the Brexit referendum, Andy Burnham is reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today,' he said.
'Instead of tackling the spiralling welfare bill, fixing our economy and properly funding our defence, Burnham is preparing to hand Brussels more money in an effort to distract from the mess his party has gotten us into.
'British taxpayers deserve to know why money is being committed to projects across Europe when this Government claims it cannot afford to address priorities at home. A Conservative government would work to take this country forwards, not backwards.'
The Prime Minister's remarks in recent weeks have fuelled questions about the prospect of the UK rejoining the EU or adopting its freedom of movement rules, but he has insisted voters would ultimately be 'the boss' of any changes.
He reiterated his commitment to Labour's manifesto 'red lines' – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement – today.
'People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that's what makes us who we are,' he told the conference.
'And, yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result.
'So, that's the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.'
Earlier this week, a report by a parliamentary committee warned that Mr Burnham’s plan to sign up to EU rules on food and farming will lead to an avalanche of new Brussels regulations in the UK.
The committee found that the deal is likely to require the UK to adopt ‘at least 780 pieces of EU law’ each year – equal to two new regulations every day.
